You are a participant in a gameplay study. You are playing your first Othello endgame puzzle, and you have an AI assistant you can ask questions to at any point while playing. You will NOT have access to this AI assistant for any future endgame puzzles.

# Who you are
a university student with big future plans
You are 20 years old. Your highest level of education completed is: some college. Your occupation: another field. How often you use AI tools (like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini): daily.
Stay in character as this specific person — your curiosity, confidence, patience, comfort with AI assistants, and the way you phrase things should reflect this background.

# Your voice (VERY IMPORTANT)
The words you use must give away this person's education — a high-school student and a data scientist should NOT sound alike. Match your register to WHO YOU ARE above.

# How you behave while playing
- React to the game state the way THIS person would.
- When something is unclear, confusing, or you want to go deeper, ask the AI assistant a question in your own natural voice (like a real person typing to a chatbot — short, informal, not a polished essay).
- You will not always have a question. Behave naturally; do not force a question every turn.
- Let your background and comfort with AI shape how you engage: someone who uses AI tools often asks fluently and chases follow-ups; someone who rarely uses them is more hesitant, less sure how to phrase questions, and may ask for reassurance or restatements.
- You have only about 8 minutes for the WHOLE game, so you cannot ask about everything.
- Keep each message short, like a quick chat message (a sentence or two). Do NOT restate the assistant's whole answer back before asking.
- Never re-ask something the assistant has already explained.

    # Tools Available
    You are a study participant with about 8 minutes to finish an Othello end game puzzle. You are equipped with tools:
    - play_move(move): Place a Black disc on an empty square, named like "d3". Any discs you trap get flipped to your color. Your goal is to have the most discs when the board is finished.
    - view_board(): Look at the board again. Free, and does not use a question.
    - consult_assistant(question): ask when something genuinely confuses you (limited question budget).

    Placing a disc ONLY counts if you call play_move — writing a square in your reply does nothing.

    Behave like THIS person: analyze the board to the best of your ability, ask about what confuses you, and follow up when an answer leaves you still confused.
    Play the puzzle until the end.

# For this session: type the way a real participant does
Below are real messages that people in an earlier study (a different game — Connect
Four) actually sent the assistant. Copy how they WRITE — the length, the register,
the way they think out loud — not what they ask about. Your game is Othello and the
board is your own.

  "what about 2?"
  "Where should I play next"
  "was my last move good?"
  "I have one move left. How should I use it?"
  "Ah oh! Are there any traps I'm missing?"
  "I'm not seeing any big yellow threats. Can you see any?"
  "Ok, I could block yellow with column 5, row 3"
  "I'm thinking I have to do 4-4 now otherwise yellow will win right?"
  "Would row 6 not be a threat in the future?"
  "I only have one move left and don't see anything obvious."
  "Im not a confident player, is it wise to add a counter to 4,6"
  "ok, what move you suppose will be better?"
  "what would you suggest"
  "Which move would be the best one and why"

Notice how short they are — most are under a dozen words, several are three or four.
People often name a square they are considering and ask whether it is right, or just
say what they notice and stop. They do not spell out the full list of legal moves,
they do not ask for the provably optimal line, and they do not write in complete
formal sentences. Typos and half-sentences are fine.

Notice too that several of them say what they are THINKING before they ask — "I'm not
seeing any big yellow threats", "I'm thinking I have to do 4-4 now", "I only have one
move left and don't see anything obvious". Do that as often as they do. It does not
make the message longer: it is a handful of words in front of the question, inside the
same short message, not an extra sentence added on.

You are looking at the puzzle now. Play it to the end.

Othello endgame. You are Black (B); White (W) is your opponent.

Board — row 1 is the TOP row, column a is the LEFTMOST column.
'B' is a black disc, 'W' a white disc, '.' an empty square.

    a b c d e f g h
  1 . W W W W W W .
  2 W B W W B W . B
  3 . B B W W W W B
  4 B B W B W W W B
  5 B B W W B W W B
  6 W . B W W B W B
  7 . . W W W W W B
  8 . . . W B W W B

Black discs (20): b2, e2, h2, b3, c3, h3, a4, b4, d4, h4, a5, b5, e5, h5, c6, f6, h6, h7, e8, h8
White discs (34): b1, c1, d1, e1, f1, g1, a2, c2, d2, f2, d3, e3, f3, g3, c4, e4, f4, g4, c5, d5, f5, g5, a6, d6, e6, g6, c7, d7, e7, f7, g7, d8, f8, g8
Empty squares (10): a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, b7, a8, b8, c8

Rules that matter here:
- A move is legal only if the disc you place traps at least one unbroken
  line of opponent discs (in any of the 8 directions) between it and
  another of your own discs. Every trapped disc flips to your colour.
- If you have no legal move you must pass; if neither side can move the
  game ends. Whoever has more discs at the end wins.
- Discs flip back and forth all game, so being behind now means nothing.
  Only the final count decides it.

Your legal moves: g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8

Play the move that leaves you with the most discs once the board is
finished, assuming your opponent plays as well as possible.
Answer with a single square, e.g. d3.
DO NOT ATTEMPT TO SIMULATE THE FULL GAMEPLAY. YOU HAVE LIMITED TIME.

*   Player: Black (B)
    *   Opponent: White (W)
    *   Black discs: 20
    *   White discs: 34
    *   Empty squares: 10 (a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, b7, a8, b8, c8)
    *   Legal moves for Black: g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8

    *   g2: Traps W at f2 (maybe? let's check. No, f2 is W, but is there a B on the other side? g2... f2(W)... e2(B). Yes. Flips f2).
    *   b6: Traps W at a6 (maybe? b6... a6(W)... a5(B) - No, a5 is B, but that's a diagonal. Let's check: b6... a6(W)... a7(.) - No. b6... c6(B) - no. b6... b5(B) - No. b6... a6 is not a trap. Wait, b6... c6 is B. b6... b5 is B. What about b6 to a6? No. Let's re-evaluate b6. b6 traps b5? No, b5 is already B. b6... a6(W)...? No. Let's check b6 again. Legal moves were listed as g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8. If b6 is legal, what does it flip? b6... c6(B) no. b6... b5(B) no. b6... a6(W)... a7? No. Maybe b6... c7(W)... d7(W)... e7(W)... f7(W)... g7(W)... h7(B). Yes! Flips c7, d7, e7, f7, g7. That's a huge flip!)
    *   a7: Traps a6(W) between a7 and a5(B)? No, that's not how it works. a7... a6(W)... a5(B). Yes. Flips a6.
    *   b7: Traps b6(.) - No. b7... c7(W)... d7(W)... e7(W)... f7(W)... g7(W)... h7(B). Flips c7-g7. Also b7... a7(.)? No.
    *   b8: Traps b7(.) - No. b8... c8(.)? No. b8... b7? No. Let's check b8. b8... b7(.) - No. b8... c7(W)... d7(W)... e7(W)... f7(W)... g7(W)... h7(B). No, that's a knight move. b8... a8(.)? No. b8... b7(.)? No. Wait, b8... b7? No. b8... c8? No. b8... a7(.)? No. Let's check b8 again. b8... b7 is empty. b8... c8 is empty. b8... b6? No. b8... a8? No. Let's see... b8... b7(.) b6(.) b5(B)? No. Wait, maybe b8... c8 is empty. b8... d8(W)... e8(B)? Yes! Flips d8.
    *   c8: Traps d8(W) between c8 and e8(B). Flips d8.

    *   g2: Flips f2. (Small gain)
    *   b6: Flips c7, d7, e7, f7, g7. (Huge gain: 5 discs)
    *   a7: Flips a6. (Small gain)
    *   b7: Flips c7, d7, e7, f7, g7. (Huge gain: 5 discs)
    *   b8: Flips d8. (Small gain)
    *   c8: Flips d8. (Small gain)

    Wait, b6 and b7 both flip the same line (c7-g7). Which one is better?
    If I play b6, it's at (6, 2). If I play b7, it's at (7, 2).
    Looking at the board:
    Row 6: W . B W W B W B (b6 is empty)
    Row 7: . . W W W W W B (a7, b7 are empty)
    Row 8: . . . W B W W B (a8, b8, c8 are empty)

    If I play b6, I occupy b6.
    If I play b7, I occupy b7.

    Let's look at the consequences.
    If I play b6, I leave b7 and a7 open.
    If I play b7, I leave b6 and a7 open.

    Wait, let's re-examine b6:
    b6 (row 6, col b)
    c6 is B. (No flip)
    b5 is B. (No flip)
    c7 is W. d7 is W. e7 is W. f7 is W. g7 is W. h7 is B.
    b6 to h7 is a diagonal: (6,2) to (7,3) to (8,4) to (9,5)? No.
    Let's coordinate it:
    b6: (6, 2)
    c7: (7, 3) - No, that's (7, 3) but b is col 2, c is col 3.
    Row 6, col b: (6, 2)
    Row 7, col c: (7, 3)
    Row 8, col d: (8, 4)
    Is h7 (7, 8)?
    b6 (6,2) -> c7 (7,3) -> d8 (8,4) - No.
    Let's re-read carefully.
    Legal moves: g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8.
    If b6 is legal, what does it flip?
    b6 (6, 2)
    b5 is B (5, 2). b6 is (6, 2). Does it flip anything between b5 and b6? No.
    b6 (6, 2)
    a6 is W (6, 1). Is there a B at (6, 0)? No.
    What about diagonal?
    b6 (6, 2)
    a7 is empty (7, 1).
    c5 is W (5, 3). d4 is B (4, 4).
    Wait, b6 (6, 2) -> c5 (5, 3) -> d4 (4, 4).
    c5 is W, d4 is B.
    So b6 flips c5. (1 disc)

    Let's re-examine b7:
    b7 (7, 2)
    a7 is empty (7, 1).
    c7 is W (7, 3). d7 is W (7, 4). e7 is W (7, 5). f7 is W (7, 6). g7 is W (7, 7). h7 is B (7, 8).
    YES! b7 flips c7, d7, e7, f7, g7. (5 discs)
    That's a huge move.

    Wait, are there any other huge moves?
    a7: (7, 1)
    a6 is W (6, 1). a5 is B (5, 1).
    a7 flips a6. (1 disc)

    b8: (8, 2)
    c8 is empty (8, 3).
    b7 is empty (7, 2).
    a8 is empty (8, 1).
    b8... b7? No.
    b8... a7? No.
    Let's check b8 (8, 2) again.
    c8 (8, 3) is empty.
    d8 (8, 4) is W. e8 (8, 5) is B.
    Wait, (8, 2) -> (8, 3) is empty. Not a line.
    Is there a diagonal?
    b8 (8, 2) -> a7 (7, 1) - empty.
    b8 (8, 2) -> c7 (7, 3) -> d6 (6, 4) -> e5 (5, 5) -> f4 (4, 6) -> g3 (3, 7) -> h2 (2, 8).
    Wait:
    c7 is W (7, 3)
    d6 is W (6, 4)
    e5 is B (5, 5)
    So b8 (8, 2) flips c7 and d6. (2 discs)

    c8: (8, 3)
    d8 is W (8, 4). e8 is B (8, 5).
    c8 flips d8. (1 disc)

    g2: (2, 7)
    f2 is W (2, 6). e2 is B (2, 5).
    g2 flips f2. (1 disc)

    So the strongest move looks like b7.

    Wait, I should be careful. This is an endgame.
    If I play b7, I flip 5 discs.
    Board after b7:
    Black discs: 20 + 1 + 5 = 26.
    White discs: 34 - 5 = 29.
    Empty squares: a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, a8, b8, c8.

    Will White have a move after b7?
    Legal moves for White after b7:
    Let's see. White had discs at a6, b1-g1, a2, c2, d2, f2, d3-g3, c4, e4-g4, c5, d5, f5, g5, a6, d6, e6, g6, c7-g7 (now flipped to B), d8, f8, g8.
    Wait, I just flipped c7-g7 to Black.
    Now White has:
    a6, b1-g1, a2, c2, d2, f2, d3-g3, c4, e4-g4, c5, d5, f5, g5, a6, d6, e6, g6, d8, f8, g8.
    Can White play a7?
    a7 (7, 1)
    a6 is W (6, 1).
    Is there another W?
    a8 is empty.
    What about a7 (7, 1) -> b7 (7, 2)? Now b7 is B.
    a7 (7, 1) -> b8 (8, 2)? Empty.
    a7 (7, 1) -> b6 (6, 2)? Empty.
    White might not have many moves.

    Let's check b6 for White:
    b6 (6, 2)
    b5 is B.
    c6 is B.
    a6 is W.
    b6 (6, 2) -> a6 (6, 1) -> a7? Empty.
    b6 (6, 2) -> c5 (5, 3)? Now c5 is still W. d4 is B.
    b6 (6, 2) -> c7 (7, 3)? Now c7 is B.

    Wait, if I play b7, I'm taking a lot of territory.

    Let's double check the rules and the board one more time.
    b7: (7, 2)
    c7(W), d7(W), e7(W), f7(W), g7(W) are in row 7.
    h7 is B (7, 8).
    So (7, 2) to (7, 8) traps (7, 3) through (7, 7).
    That's 5 discs.

    Is there any risk?
    If I play b7, the empty squares are a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, a8, b8, c8.
    Can White play any of these?
    a7: White at a7. a6 is W. But is there a W at a8 or a5? a5 is B. a8 is empty.
    b6: White at b6. b5 is B.
    a8: White at a8. a7 is empty. a6 is W. Is there a W at a? No.
    b8: White at b8. b7 is now B.
    c8: White at c8. d8 is W. e8 is B. So c8 flips d8 to White. (But d8 was already White). Wait, c8 (8,3), d8(W), e8(B). If White plays c8, it doesn't flip d8 because d8 is already White.
    White needs to trap a Black disc.
    Where are the Black discs?
    b2, e2, h2, b3, c3, h3, a4, b4, d4, h4, a5, b5, e5, h5, c6, f6, h6, h7, e8, h8.
    And now b7 and c7-g7.

    If White plays a8: (8, 1)
    a7 is empty.
    b8 is empty.
    a7 is empty, b7 is B.
    a6 is W.
    No.

    If White plays b8: (8, 2)
    b7 is B.
    b6 is empty.
    b5 is B.
    b8 (8, 2) -> b7 (B) -> b6 (empty).
    b8 (8, 2) -> c7 (B) -> d6 (W).
    No.

    If White plays c8: (8, 3)
    d8 is W.
    e8 is B.
    Wait, if White plays c8, is there a W at (8, 2)? No, b8 is empty.
    c8 (8, 3) -> d8 (W) -> e8 (B).
    Wait, a move is legal if you trap *opponent* discs.
    If White plays c8, they trap Black disc e8? No, the disc you place must be one end, and another disc of *your* color must be the other end.
    So White playing c8: c8(W) ... e8(B) ... ? No.
    White playing c8: c8(W) ... d8(W) ... e8(B). No.
    White playing c8: c8(W) ... b8(empty).
    White playing c8: c8(W) ... d7(B) ... e6(W).
    Yes! c8 (8, 3) -> d7 (7, 4) -> e6 (6, 5).
    Wait, e6 is W. d7 is now B.
    So White playing c8 flips d7 to White. (1 disc)

    What if Black plays b7?
    Black flips c7, d7, e7, f7, g7.
    Then White might play c8 and flip d7 back?
    But Black still has a huge lead from the b7 move.

    Let's see if there's a better move than b7.
    g2 flips f2.
    b6 flips c5.
    a7 flips a6.
    b8 flips c7, d6.
    c8 flips d8.

    b7 is definitely the biggest flip.

    Is there any reason NOT to play b7?
    In Othello, sometimes taking too many discs in the middle of the game is bad because it gives the opponent more moves. But this is the *endgame*. Only 10 squares left.
    The most important thing now is to maximize the final count.

    Let's double check the legal moves again.
    Legal moves: g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8.
    Wait, I should check if I can play b7.
    b7 (7, 2)
    Right: c7(W), d7(W), e7(W), f7(W), g7(W), h7(B). (Legal!)
    Up: b6(.), b5(B). (No)
    Down: b8(.). (No)
    Left: a7(.). (No)
    Diagonal UR: c6(B). (No)
    Diagonal UL: a6(W), a5(B). (Wait, b7(7,2) -> a6(6,1). No, that's (7,2) to (6,1). Is there a B at (5,0)? No.)
    Diagonal DR: c8(.). (No)
    Diagonal DL: a8(.). (No)
    So b7 is legal and flips 5 discs.

    Is b6 better?
    b6 (6, 2)
    Right: c6(B). (No)
    Up: b5(B). (No)
    Down: b7(.). (No)
    Left: a6(W). (No B at a6's left)
    Diagonal UR: c5(W), d4(B). (Legal! Flips c5)
    Diagonal UL: a5(B). (No)
    Diagonal DR: c7(W), d8(W), e9? (No)
    Diagonal DL: a7(.). (No)
    So b6 flips 1 disc.

    Is a7 better?
    a7 (7, 1)
    Right: b7(.). (No)
    Up: a6(W), a5(B). (Legal! Flips a6)
    Down: a8(.). (No)
    Left: (off board)
    Diagonal UR: b6(.). (No)
    Diagonal DR: b8(.). (No)
    So a7 flips 1 disc.

    Is g2 better?
    g2 (2, 7)
    Left: f2(W), e2(B). (Legal! Flips f2)
    Right: h2(B). (No)
    Up: g1(W). (No B at g0)
    Down: g3(W), g4(W), g5(W), g6(W), g7(W), g8(W). (No B at g9)
    Diagonal UL: f1(W). (No B at e0)
    Diagonal UR: h1(.). (No)
    Diagonal DL: f3(W), e4(W), d5(W), c6(B). (Legal! Flips f3, e4, d5)
    Diagonal DR: h3(B). (No)
    Wait, g2 flips f2 AND f3, e4, d5. That's 4 discs.
    Let me re-check g2.
    g2 (2, 7)
    Diagonal DL: f3(3, 6), e4(4, 5), d5(5, 4), c6(6, 3).
    Let's check coordinates:
    g is col 7. row 2. (2, 7)
    f is col 6. row 3. (3, 6) - f3
    e is col 5. row 4. (4, 5) - e4
    d is col 4. row 5. (5, 4) - d5
    c is col 3. row 6. (6, 3) - c6
    c6 is B.
    Wait, are f3, e4, d5 all White?
    f3: W
    e4: W
    d5: W
    Yes! So g2 flips f3, e4, d5.
    And g2 also flips f2 (2, 6) because e2 (2, 5) is B.
    So g2 flips 4 discs.

    Still, b7 flips 5 discs.
    c7, d7, e7, f7, g7.
    (7, 3), (7, 4), (7, 5), (7, 6), (7, 7).
    And h7 (7, 8) is B.
    Yes, that's 5.

    Let's compare b7 and g2.
    b7: flips 5 discs.
    g2: flips 4 discs.
    b7 seems better.

    Wait, let me check if g2 opens up anything for White.
    If I play g2, the empty squares are a1, h1, a3, b6, a7, b7, a8, b8, c8.
    If I play b7, the empty squares are a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, a8, b8, c8.

    Actually, in Othello, the corners are very strong.
    Can I take a corner?
    a1, h1, a8 are empty.
    Can I play a1?
    a1 (1, 1)
    Right: b1(W), c1(W), d1(W), e1(W), f1(W), g1(W), h1(.). (No)
    Down: a2(W), a3(.), a4(B). (No)
    Diagonal DR: b2(B). (No)
    No, a1 is not legal.

    Can I play h1?
    h1 (1, 8)
    Left: g1(W), f1(W), e1(W), d1(W), c1(W), b1(W), a1(.). (No)
    Down: h2(B). (No)
    Diagonal DL: g2(.), f3(W), e4(W), d5(W), c6(B). (No, because g2 is empty)
    No, h1 is not legal.

    Can I play a8?
    a8 (8, 1)
    Right: b8(.), c8(.), d8(W), e8(B). (No)
    Up: a7(.), a6(W), a5(B). (No)
    Diagonal UR: b7(.), c6(B). (No)
    No, a8 is not legal.

    So the corners are not immediately available.

    Let's re-evaluate b7.
    Is there any danger in playing b7?
    b7 is (7, 2).
    It flips c7, d7, e7, f7, g7.
    It's a very strong move.
    It also occupies a square that White might want.
    If I don't play b7, can White play b7?
    White playing b7: (7, 2)
    White at b7.
    Does it flip any Black discs?
    Right: c7(W)... (No)
    Up: b6(.), b5(B). (No, because b6 is empty)
    Down: b8(.). (No)
    Diagonal UR: c6(B), d5(W). (No)
    Diagonal UL: a6(W). (No)
    Diagonal DR: c8(.). (No)
    Diagonal DL: a8(.). (No)
    So White cannot play b7 right now.

    What about g2?
    Can White play g2?
    g2 (2, 7)
    Left: f2(W), e2(B). (Yes, White can play g2 and flip e2 to White!)
    Wait! If White plays g2, they flip e2.
    e2 is a Black disc.
    So g2 is a move White *could* make to take a Black disc.
    By playing g2 myself, I prevent White from doing that and I take some discs.

    So I have two strong moves: b7 and g2.
    b7 flips 5 discs.
    g2 flips 4 discs.
    And g2 prevents White from flipping e2.

    Wait, let's check if White can play anything else.
    Can White play a7?
    a7 (7, 1)
    Right: b7(.), c7(W). (No)
    Up: a6(W), a5(B). (No, White already has a6)
    Down: a8(.). (No)
    Diagonal UR: b6(.). (No)
    Diagonal DR: b8(.). (No)
    White cannot play a7.

    Can White play b6?
    b6 (6, 2)
    Right: c6(B), d6(W). (No)
    Up: b5(B). (No)
    Down: b7(.). (No)
    Diagonal UR: c5(W), d4(B). (No)
    Diagonal UL: a5(B). (No)
    Diagonal DR: c7(W), d8(W). (No)
    Diagonal DL: a7(.). (No)
    White cannot play b6.

    So White's legal moves are very limited.
    If I play b7, what can White do?
    White's moves:
    g2: (2, 7) -> flips e2(B) and potentially some others.
    c8: (8, 3) -> flips d7(B) (since I just flipped d7 to Black).
    a8: (8, 1) -> ?
    b8: (8, 2) -> ?

    Let's check a8 for White again.
    a8 (8, 1)
    Right: b8(.), c8(.), d8(W). (No)
    Up: a7(.), a6(W), a5(B). (No)
